The content of this document is proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as
a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training
Act 2020. Once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, it will set the
requirements for the teaching of Years 0–10 The Arts in state schools, and schools
will be required to start using it in Years 9–10 from 1 January 2027 and in Years 0–8
from 1 January 2029.
Depending on their contexts, some schools may not be ready for full implementation
on day one of the specified school year, so the following transition arrangements are
proposed to apply:
    •   For students in Years 0–8, schools will need to make a start by developing,
        and then executing, a plan that achieves full implementation as soon as
        practicable and by no later than the end of 2030.
    •   For students in Years 9–10, schools will need to make a start by developing,
        and then executing, a plan that achieves full implementation as soon as
        practicable and by no later than the end of 2027.
Implementation requirements for specified kura boards will be confirmed when the
proposed National Curriculum Statements are made under the Act and published in
the New Zealand Gazette. This is to allow more time for the Crown to engage with
Kaupapa Māori education providers through their representative bodies in advance of
these proposed decisions affecting their kura. A specified kura board means the
board of any of the following:
    •   a kura kaupapa Māori
    •   a designated character school with a character that is hapū- or iwi-based or
        that affiliates with Ngā Kura ā-Iwi o Aotearoa
    •   a state integrated school with a special character that is hapū- or iwi-based.

Purpose                                  Te toi whakairo, ka ihiihi, ka wehiwehi, ka aweawe te ao katoa.
      statement                                Artistic excellence makes the world sit up in wonder.


The Arts is a broad field of study and practice focused on human creativity, self-
expression, and cultural communication. Its purpose can be to entertain, educate, tell
stories, reflect society, and provoke thought. Included in the Arts are the disciplines of
Dance, Drama, Music, and the Visual Arts.
The Arts fosters students’ creativity and confidence, helping them express ideas,
emotions, and experiences in meaningful ways.
The Arts engages students with toi Māori and artistic practices from New Zealand, the
Pacific, and the wider world. By exploring how the arts communicate ideas and reflect
cultures, students become informed, creative citizens who contribute to cultural
understanding, community connection, and a shared sense of identity.
The Arts learning area prepares students with the knowledge and practices to access
related curriculum subjects in Years 11–13.

‘Making and creating’ and ‘Observing and responding’ in Drama and Visual Arts, and
‘Listening and responding’, ‘Performing’, ‘Improvising and composing’ and ‘Elements
of music’ in Music.
The sub-strands are designed to be taught together, not in one particular order. This
means teachers weave these sub-strands into a single learning process. Students
move fluidly between noticing how meaning is created in the arts and applying those
insights as they shape their own performances or artworks. This integrated approach
reflects how artists work and ensures students build understanding and skill at the
same time.
Framing of the practices
Across Dance, Drama, and the Visual Arts, the knowledge of both sub-strands is
enacted in the practices. In Music, the knowledge of the four sub-strands is drawn
together into shared practices within a year level.
Above each Arts strand, phase-level context statements suggest to teachers a variety
of artistic experiences that students may encounter through Dance, Drama, Music,
and Visual Arts. These relevant examples support the expectation that, across each
phase, students engage with artistic practices, works, and traditions from different
time periods and places.
The importance of community context

Teachers enrich the teaching sequence and give it meaning by connecting it to
directly relevant and visible examples from the local context: people and place, te ao
Māori, and experiences in the lives of students and their communities.
It is important to note that while the teaching sequence includes prescribed
knowledge and practices, examples and contexts that include an ‘e.g.’ are illustrative.
These examples are intended to provide guidance but not to mandate what is to be
taught. Provided the intended knowledge and practices are taught, teachers may
substitute alternative examples that better reflect local environments, community,
hapū and iwi connections, student interests, teacher expertise, or emerging issues
relating to the discipline.
